The Delacroix wedding paid in advance, in a single cashier's cheque for twenty-two thousand dollars, and Wren held it in both hands for a full minute before she let herself believe it was real.

The bride's family was from Boston and had summered on the island for three generations, and when the inn's ballroom flooded in April they had decided, with the reckless confidence of people who had never been told no, that the reception would be held aboard the *Margaret Ann* on a slow circuit of Gullet Sound. Wren had quoted a number she thought was insane. The bride's mother had said, "Is that all?"

So for five hours on the twenty-third of May, the old ferry was a floating ballroom. Tobias and two of the Gunderson boys strung white lights along the rails. A string quartet sat in the passenger cabin, damp and gallant. There were oysters on ice in fish crates, and a cake shaped like the Gullet lighthouse, and a hundred and ten guests in linen who kept asking Wren if she was *the captain*, and she kept saying yes.

At sunset, with the quartet playing something sad and gorgeous and the bride dancing barefoot on the foredeck, Tobias climbed into the wheelhouse with two glasses of champagne someone had pressed on him.

"Twenty-two," he said, handing her one.

"Twenty-two." She did not drink it. She was driving. But she held it. "Plus the cruises. Plus the skiff. We're at sixty-four, Toby. Sixty-four. That's more than half."

"Dad never cleared twenty-two in a day in his life."

"Dad never charged anyone enough." She was smiling, she realized. Her face felt strange with it. "If we can book two more of these before the end of June, and keep the cruises full—"

"We could actually do it."

"We could actually do it."

He clinked his glass against hers. Below them, the wedding guests whooped as the groom dipped the bride under the white lights, and the water of Gullet Sound was copper and rose and perfectly calm, and for one hour Wren Halloway believed in arithmetic again.

The black car was waiting at the head of the pier when they docked.

Corwin Pell did not get out. A younger man did: a narrow, polite man in a gray suit, who introduced himself as Mr. Albrecht, counsel for Pell Coastal Holdings, and handed Wren an envelope while the last wedding guests were still stumbling up the pier with their shoes in their hands.

"A courtesy notice," Mr. Albrecht said. "Paragraph eleven of your father's note. The acceleration clause."

Wren opened the envelope under the sodium lamp. Tobias read over her shoulder.

*In the event of the death or incapacity of the Borrower, the Lender may, at its sole discretion, declare the entire unpaid principal immediately due and payable upon ten (10) days' written notice.*

"Ten days," Tobias said. "Ten *days*?"

"Mr. Pell has been patient," said Mr. Albrecht. "Out of respect for your family's loss. But he notes that your circumstances have changed—that you are, it seems, trying to pay." He said it as though it were faintly vulgar. "The full amount is now due on the second of June. One hundred and twenty thousand dollars. The day after the council vote, as it happens."

"You can't do that," Wren said.

"Paragraph eleven says we can." He nodded to them both. "Good evening. Congratulations on the wedding."

The car drove off. The white lights were still burning along the rails of the *Margaret Ann*. Out on the foredeck, a bridesmaid had fallen asleep on a coil of rope, holding a slice of lighthouse cake.

Wren folded the notice into precise thirds, the way she folded invoices, and put it in her pocket.

"Sixty-four," she said. "Out of a hundred and twenty. In ten days."

Tobias didn't answer. He went down to the foredeck, and very gently woke the bridesmaid, and helped her up the pier to find her friends.
